narrative:
Seven specialists produced seven maps of the same territory, and the cross-dataset audit showed most of them were tracing the same four source-pools. The value left on the table is therefore not inside any one domain. It is in the pairs of facts that no single domain could hold at once, and I hunted specifically for pairs whose halves come from disciplines that never meet: a federation rulebook and a B2B channel P&L; a sweat-physiology paper and a claims regulation; a national participation registry and a sun-protection standard; a competitor's football quarter and a basketball line plan.

Four things fell out.

First, the rulebook is the only thing in this entire evidence base that actually CHANGED. Fifty-eight surviving signals describe stable conditions, stale numbers or contested trends. Two items are new, dated, primary and verified - NFHS Rule 3-4-5 for 2025-26, permitting teammates to wear multiple STYLES of like-coloured uniform bottoms (shorts, pants, skirts), and FIBA's official interpretation that compression undershorts are legal at ANY length provided the team matches colour. Both surfaced inside A06-S3, and both were found by the skeptic rather than the specialist. They matter for a commercial reason no athlete analyst would reach for: uniform bottoms are ordered by coaches through team dealers against a compliance spec (A04-S9). Before the change, a longer or different bottom was a per-athlete permission request, which is un-orderable as a stock SKU. After it, a like-coloured multi-style bottoms family is orderable. That converts the coverage-first need (A05-S8) and the layering behaviour (A06-S6) from consumer preferences into channel-legal product, and it lands squarely on the consumer group where Nike's mindshare fell hardest (A01-S1).

Second, everything in this base is specified dry and used wet. Basketball uniforms trap 0.00-1.33 kg of sweat, rising with intensity (A06-S2). Polyester's UPF 40-50 rating is a dry-state measurement, and the single peer-reviewed paper on the subject is about what moisture does to it (A06-S7). Drawstrings slip when saturated; the reproducible consumer complaints are seams and shrinkage after laundering (A01-S3, A01-S2). The wet garment is the object nobody has tested, and it is the one place a performance claim would still be defensible as claims regimes tighten (A03-S5).

Third, the white spaces were visibility failures, not product gaps. The DNA UV Woven already carries UV protection, a phone-secure zip pocket and a durability claim (A03-S7, A06-S4, A07-S8) - and seven diligent researchers with full search access could not find it. That is a hard measurement of invisibility. Local labels win precisely by printing their function and their place on the OUTSIDE of the garment (A07-S9), while the channel swings to wholesale racks that carry no product copy at all (A02-S7).

Fourth, the portfolio is weighted inversely to its evidence. Australia is the best-verified non-US market in the base and supports no opportunity (A02-S9); Greater China carries the most opportunities and not one retrieved Chinese price (A02-S2, A02-S3, A04-S2). I have written candidates against that inversion rather than around it.

Every candidate below is a hypothesis, not a finding. Where the evidence argues against it, I have named the signal that does so rather than averaging it away.

patterns.title: The rulebook is the only dataset that changed - and it changed in favour of women, layering and the team channel
patterns.description: Across 58 surviving signals, almost everything is either stable (physiology, court dimensions, retail structure), stale (2019 PR estimates, 2024 league releases, 2014 quotes) or contested (inseam direction, market size, China). Exactly two items are new, dated, primary and verified: NFHS Rule 3-4-5 (2025-26) permitting teammates to wear multiple STYLES of like-coloured uniform bottoms so religious and personal accommodations no longer require a permission request, and FIBA's official interpretation that compression undershorts are legal at ANY length provided the team matches colour. Both sit inside A06-S3 and both were surfaced by the skeptic, not the specialist. The non-obvious step is commercial rather than technical: team bottoms are bought by coaches through dealers against a compliance spec (A04-S9), so a rule that widens what counts as compliant is the thing that makes a non-standard bottom orderable at all. A rules change is a demand-enabling event in a B2B channel in a way it never is in DTC, and it lands on exactly the consumer where Nike's mindshare erosion is concentrated (A01-S1) and where non-US participation is growing fastest (A02-S9).

patterns.title: Every claimed white space is a visibility failure, and seven researchers failing to find a shipped SKU is the measurement
patterns.description: Four separate 'gaps' - outdoor function (A03-S7), secure storage (A06-S4), composed outdoor system (A07-S8) and UV (A06-S7) - are all closed by one inline Nike SKU that carries UVA/UVB protection, side pockets, a zippered utility pocket sized for a phone and a woven face marketed against rebound battles. The interesting fact is not that the product exists; it is that seven independent researchers with unrestricted search could not see it, and that the same researchers had no difficulty seeing Li-Ning's UPF 50+ Wade platform, Ugat's flag-printed Watawat short and Li-Ning BadFive. The difference is that the competitors' function and place are printed on the outside of the garment while Nike's are described only in PDP copy. That becomes a commercial problem specifically now, because distribution is swinging to wholesale racks where there is no copy at all (A02-S7) and Nike Digital - the only surface where the copy lives - has declined for ten consecutive quarters. Legibility, not capability, is the gap.

patterns.title: The garment is specified dry and used wet; every unresolved failure mode lives in the saturated state
patterns.description: Read across disciplines, the failure modes cluster in one physical condition nobody tested. Basketball uniforms trap 0.00-1.33 kg of sweat, rising with intensity and with a wider range than treadmill running (A06-S2). Peer-reviewed testing shows 100% polyester technical sportswear already rates UPF 40-50+ untreated - but that is a dry rating, and the paper's actual subject is what moisture and sweat do to it (A06-S7). Drawstrings are reported to slip when saturated. The reproducible consumer complaints are seams failing and shrinkage after a single wash (A01-S3, A01-S2), which is a post-wet-state defect. Meanwhile the priority use case is 27-32C high-humidity outdoor play (A06-S5). So the entire spec conversation - GSM, UPF, abrasion, dry-time - is conducted on a dry garment while the entire consumer conversation is about a soaked one. This is invisible to any single specialist because the sweat number lives in sports science, the UV degradation in textile chemistry, the seam failure in retail reviews and the humidity in climate data.

patterns.title: Full-price demand concentrates where people physically gather, while the promotional floor sits where product is planned
patterns.description: Two datasets that never meet say the same thing. On the commercial side, the US wholesale marketplace is described as increasingly promotional with Foot Locker comps -3.6% and Nike citing elevated markdowns (A04-S4), and Nike's own ASP gain is mix rather than pricing power (A03-S9). On the culture side, the live-event economy is doing the opposite: Unrivaled's Philadelphia night generated roughly USD 1M in tickets AND USD 400,000 in merchandise while its broadcast viewership fell 9% (A05-S7); the NBL ran a third consecutive million-plus season with 58-63 sellouts (A05-S6, A02-S9); Quai 54 moved into Roland-Garros. Event retail is a full-price channel hiding inside a promotional market, and it is the only place in this evidence base where a shorts buy has a demonstrated reason to sell at full price. No specialist connected them because attendance data is a cultural artefact and markdown rate is a finance artefact.

patterns.title: Nike's inseam-price ladder is inverted against three of its own priority consumers at once
patterns.description: The longest, most-covering, most size-inclusive SKU in the men's line - the DNA Academy 11-inch, including Big and Tall - is also the cheapest, at roughly USD 37, while the 6-inch sits at USD 65 (A02-S5, A07-S4, A02-S4). That single architectural fact collides with three separate consumer findings none of which was read next to it: the coverage-first need among taller women and modest-dressing athletes (A05-S8), the plus-size and value replenishment behaviour that AND1 serves up to 5XL (A01-S9), and the retro lifestyle pole that Hibbett defines as 9 inches or longer (A05-S3). So the length that three under-served groups want is positioned as the line's basement product, in the cheapest fabric, with no women's grading, at a price point that trains the consumer to read coverage as cheapness. The inversion is invisible because inseam data sits in marketplace, modesty in culture, plus-size in consumer and price in commercial.

patterns.title: The sewn-in liner is the one component three disciplines independently want deleted, and deleting it funds the fix a fourth demands
patterns.description: Three separate lines of evidence converge on the same component without any of them naming the other two. Athlete: serious players layer 3/4 or full compression under shorts, making the brief liner redundant and hotter (A06-S6), and FIBA explicitly permits compression undershorts at any length with team colour matching (A06-S3). Physiology: the liner is the densest fabric mass in the garment and the garment already traps up to 1.33 kg of sweat (A06-S2), in a use case that is 27-32C and humid (A06-S5). Commercial: the volume franchise draws seam-failure and 'paper-thin' complaints (A04-S6, A01-S3) at a price point that could not be raised because everything under USD 100 was exempted from the June 2025 action (A04-S8). Deleting a component that two consumer groups do not want is a cost-down that pays for the fabric and seam construction the third group is complaining about, at an unchanged ticket. That is a P&L move discovered in a physiology dataset.

patterns.title: The portfolio is weighted inversely to the quality of its evidence: the best-verified market carries no opportunity, the least-verified carries the most
patterns.description: Australia is the single best-verified non-US signal in the entire base - roughly 1.3 million players, second among team participation sports, female participation +25% since 2022 past 450,000, an estimated 150,000 players turned away for lack of court space, NBL attendance over 1.2 million with 58-63 sellouts, and a league on-court partner (Champion) that is not a performance-basketball leader (A02-S9, A05-S6). Every skeptic correction ran in its favour. It supports one signal and zero dedicated opportunities. Greater China, by contrast, carries the largest share of the portfolio on evidence that is geographically displaced at source (European and US reseller pages, a JD aggregator, a 2019 league PR estimate), in Nike's worst-performing region (A02-S2 at -13% currency-neutral, apparel units -8%), inside a contracting branded basketball segment (A02-S3 Li-Ning basketball -19%, contradicted by A04-S2 at +5% in H1 2026), with the route to market narrowing as Topsports exits online. No single specialist could see this because each held only its own geography weighting; it only appears when the seven files are counted together.

candidates.name: Like-Coloured: a rules-legal team bottoms system, not a team short
candidates.thesis: A 2025-26 US high-school rule change made multiple STYLES of like-coloured uniform bottoms legal on the same team for the first time, which converts coverage, modesty and layering from per-athlete permission requests into an orderable team-dealer SKU family - so Nike should sell a colour-matched bottoms SYSTEM (game short, 3/4 tight, full-length pant) rather than a better team short.
candidates.intersection: sports-governance rulebooks x team-dealer channel economics x women's and modest-dress fit need
candidates.target_consumer: US high-school and club/AAU programmes ordering through team dealers (BSN and peers), with the athlete beneficiaries being girls and women who want coverage, modest-dressing Muslim athletes, and players who already layer 3/4 compression - plus the coaches and athletic directors who actually place the order and who previously had to file a permission request to field a mixed set.
candidates.why_nike: This is a channel and compliance play, and Nike's advantages there are structural rather than creative: it already reaches the dealer channel, it can build one chassis with one colour card across three bottom styles, and the bottleneck being removed is a rule, not a design problem. It converts the Uniform of Youth and Women's Revolution priority spaces into a single bookings-led, low-markdown programme in the one channel evidence describes as growing with reliable reorder economics (A04-S9), rather than another SKU on a promotional wholesale rack (A04-S4). It also directly addresses the consumer where Nike's mindshare loss is concentrated (A01-S1) without requiring a new fabric platform.
candidates.why_hard_to_see: It requires reading an NFHS rules-change release and a B2B distributor's bookings economics in the same sentence. The rule change appears in this base only as skeptic counter-evidence inside an athlete signal about rulebooks (A06-S3); the channel fact sits in a commercial signal that contains no basketball-shorts data at all (A04-S9); the human need sits in a culture signal built on 2014-2017 evidence (A05-S8). Every specialist that touched one of these treated it as background. A PLM reading any single domain file would see a rules constraint, a distributor profile, or an inclusion story - never a demand-enabling event.
candidates.risks: The rule is US high-school only; FIBA and NCAA have not made the equivalent change, and France bans hijab in federated play, so the addressable set is narrower than the inclusion story implies. Prevalence of compression layering below elite level is entirely unmeasured. Nobody has counted how many programmes would actually order a mixed set, and multi-style ordering could raise dealer complexity and fill-rate risk rather than lower it. The claim that Nike's existing team short is competitively weak is asserted in A04-O4 with zero evidence and is trivially checkable against BSN's published catalogue.

candidates.name: Wet-State Spec: sun and heat protection certified soaked, not dry
candidates.thesis: Polyester basketball shorts already test UPF 40-50+ untreated when dry, so the only defensible sun-and-heat claim left is a wet-state one - certify UPF, dry-time and dimensional stability at the 1.33 kg of sweat the garment actually traps, and own a spec no competitor currently states.
candidates.intersection: sweat physiology x textile UV chemistry x tightening environmental-and-performance claims regulation
candidates.target_consumer: Hot-climate outdoor players in Southern China, the Philippines, India, the Gulf, the US Sun Belt and Australia who play multi-hour sessions or tournament days at 28-35C and are soaked within the first game - the Worldball Innovation consumer, plus the tournament organiser and school system that has to make a heat-safety decision (CVIRAA has already moved meets away from 9am-3pm).
candidates.why_nike: Nike is the only brand in this base with the testing infrastructure to certify a wet-state claim to AS/NZS 4399 or EN 13758-2 and the scale to make it a platform rather than a hangtag. It also solves a live compliance exposure rather than adding one: as generic and uncertified claims are squeezed (EmpCo applies from 27 September 2026 in the EU per A03-S5), a measured, third-party-testable wet-state number is exactly the kind of claim that survives while '70% recycled' does not. And it converts an already-shipping but invisible product (A03-S7, the DNA UV Woven) into a franchise with a proof point, instead of inventing a new one.
candidates.why_hard_to_see: The two halves live in different literatures that never cite each other. The trapped-sweat number (0.00-1.33 kg, intensity-dependent) is buried in a physiology paper that A06 cited by title and never used; the observation that polyester is already UPF 40-50 dry and that moisture is the open variable comes from a textile-science paper that only surfaced as skeptic counter-evidence against A06-S7. Read separately, one says 'basketball is a moderate-sweat sport' and the other says 'UPF is free on polyester' - two reasons NOT to build a product. Read together, they say the entire category's sun claim is measured in a state the consumer is never in.
candidates.risks: The wet-state effect may be small or may run the wrong way, in which case there is no claim and the programme is a test budget with no product. Concrete and asphalt UV albedo is 2-15%, among the lowest of outdoor surfaces, so 'court UV' is a weak consumer story on its own (A06-S7). There is no evidence that UPF drives basketball-shorts purchase anywhere outside Australia. And the whole outdoor framing rests on 'play is shifting to dawn and dusk' evidence that the skeptic showed is sourced to a court-builder's sales blog and a property listing (A06-S5), which would undercut a daytime sun claim entirely.

candidates.name: Southern Court: Australia-first outdoor programme, then Sun Belt and Gulf
candidates.thesis: Australia is the only market in the entire evidence base where verified participation growth, an existing consumer literacy for sun protection, a national UPF testing standard, a non-performance on-court incumbent and a league at real attendance scale all coexist - which makes it the correct proving ground for the Worldball outdoor short, not China.
candidates.intersection: national participation registry x sun-protection culture and certification standard x competitor weakness in a league property
candidates.target_consumer: Australian recreational and club players 14-35, disproportionately the female cohort that has grown 25% since 2022 past 450,000, plus NBL and NBA fans buying through Rebel, JD and Foot Locker AU - and, on proof, the same product logic exported to the US Sun Belt and the Gulf.
candidates.why_nike: This is a low-risk, high-evidence route to the Worldball priority space in a market where Nike already has doors and where the on-court league partner is Champion, an apparel brand rather than a performance-basketball leader (A02-S9). It is also the one market where a UPF claim is culturally understood rather than needing to be taught: the same signal that undermines UPF as a global differentiator (A06-S7) records that UPF sleeves are 'culturally accepted' in Australia while UPF shorts are not yet common. And it is a wholesale-shaped opportunity in a moment when Nike wholesale is growing and digital has declined for ten straight quarters (A02-S7).
candidates.why_hard_to_see: Australia appears in exactly one signal across seven files and supports zero opportunities, so no domain had a reason to look at it twice. The facts that make it decisive are split four ways: participation and the Champion gap sit in marketplace, the sun-protection culture and the ARPANSA UPF 50+ standard sit in an athlete signal that concludes UPF is nearly worthless, the attendance scale sits in culture, and the channel shape sits in commercial. Each domain saw a fragment that looked minor; only the stack looks like a market. The audit found the same inversion independently.
candidates.risks: Australia is small in absolute revenue terms and cannot on its own justify a global platform investment; the case depends on it being a proving ground that exports. Champion's incumbency is a league on-court contract that runs through NBL26 and is not open. UPF may be free on polyester (A06-S7), collapsing the differentiator. And no Australian retail sell-through, price ladder or basketball-shorts unit data exists anywhere in this base - the market evidence is participation and attendance, not commerce.

candidates.name: Delete the Liner, Buy the Seam: a linerless core reset funded by a component nobody wants
candidates.thesis: The sewn-in brief liner is redundant for players who layer compression (explicitly rules-legal at any length) and actively harmful for hot-humid outdoor play, so removing it releases cost and wet-weight inside a frozen sub-USD-100 price ladder and pays for the seam construction and dimensional stability that are the actual reproducible consumer complaints.
candidates.intersection: elite layering behaviour and FIBA rules interpretation x sweat-trapping garment physiology x a frozen price ladder and a documented quality complaint
candidates.target_consumer: Two populations that never appear on the same brief: competitive high-school, club and college players who wear 3/4 or full tights under their shorts and get no benefit from a second brief, and hot-climate outdoor recreational players for whom the liner is the densest wet mass in the garment. Commercially the buyer is the Icon and DNA core-franchise consumer, men 16-35, in wholesale doors.
candidates.why_nike: It is the rare product decision that improves the athlete experience and the gross margin in the same move, at an unchanged ticket, in a category where Nike could not take price (A04-S8) and where the quality signal is genuinely weak (Icon+ 6 inch at 3.9 stars with 67% recommending across 64 reviews, A04-S6). It also gives the linerless SKU a rules-legal system partner - a colour-matched compression tight - which connects it to C-NONOBVIOUS-1 and to the team channel. Nike owns the returns and warranty data needed to prove the payback, and nobody else in this base can make a durability claim from measurement.
candidates.why_hard_to_see: The liner is invisible in every domain that matters. Athlete intelligence saw layering behaviour but framed it as a fit and waistband-grip problem (A06-S6). Commercial saw a markdown and a durability complaint and reached for fabric GSM (A04-S6, A04-O3). Nobody costed the liner, and nobody noticed that the physiological argument for removing it (trapped sweat mass, heat in 28-32C humidity), the competitive-rules argument for removing it (FIBA permits compression undershorts at any length with colour matching), and the P&L argument for removing it all point at the same component from three unconnected files.
candidates.risks: Compression prevalence below elite level is completely unmeasured; the 'nearly every starter' claim traces to an annually re-dated SEO guide, and the only real survey (n=512) is 88% endurance athletes (A06-S6). A linerless short may simply be a worse product for the majority who wear nothing underneath, and could cannibalise higher-margin lined styles. Critically, nobody has established that fabric GSM was ever reduced (A04-S6), so the premise that there is a cost-down to reverse may be false - and if the complaints are a fit or expectation problem, this fixes nothing. The claim that prices are frozen is also superseded: Nike has taken apparel prices up 3% (A04-S8).

candidates.name: The Game-Day Bottom: the missing half of a jersey outfit, sold in fan and event doors
candidates.thesis: The women's basketball demand signal is jersey-led, not shorts-led, and the fastest-growing search behaviour is people trying to assemble an OUTFIT around a replica jersey - so the opportunity is a bottom engineered to make an oversized jersey look intentional, merchandised and priced as fan-and-event product rather than on the performance wall.
candidates.intersection: platform search-and-save behaviour x live-event merchandise economics x a performance SKU's actual reported use occasion
candidates.target_consumer: Women 16-35 attending or dressing for women's basketball - WNBA, Unrivaled, NCAA - who already own or want a replica jersey and have no considered lower half; plus the broader group buying basketball shorts as an all-occasion garment (Emily Ratajkowski and Zoe Kravitz styling long pairs with flats and kitten heels), and the reviewers who report wearing Sabrina shorts at home more than on court.
candidates.why_nike: Nike holds the WNBA on-court rights, the signature athletes and the jersey itself, which means it is the only brand that can design the bottom against its own top and sell the pair. The demand evidence is real and now durable across three seasons with a settled CBA, and the live-event channel is the one place in this evidence base with demonstrated full-price merchandise conversion (roughly USD 400,000 in one Philadelphia night, A05-S7). It reframes the women's shorts question away from an 'empty category' claim that is demonstrably false - Nike ships ISoFly, Crossover, Fly Crossover, Sabrina, WNBA Victory and Rebel Fanwear shorts - toward a job nobody is doing.
candidates.why_hard_to_see: It requires reading the Pinterest data AGAINST the inference the culture domain drew from it. A05 used jersey-search growth as evidence that consumers want shorts (A05-T2); the strongest term in the dataset (+494%) is for jersey outfits, which argues for tops. The correct reading only appears when that is put next to a product-domain review finding buried in skeptic counter-evidence - that Sabrina buyers wear the shorts at home rather than on court, so the USD 65 willingness-to-pay is lifestyle-driven - and next to an event-retail number the culture specialist missed entirely. Three files each held one third of the insight and each drew a performance conclusion from it.
candidates.risks: The Pinterest wave is pan-sport: F1 aesthetic outfit +483% and Brazil jersey outfit women +302% grow as fast as or faster than the WNBA terms, so attributing it to basketball is unsupported (A05-S4). It is search-and-save on a female-skewing platform, a leading indicator and not purchase. The WNBA growth numbers in the base are two years stale and mis-transcribed (A05-S1). Demand is still concentrated in one athlete, and the whole thesis would be settled cheaply and might be killed by splitting the Unrivaled USD 400,000 by category - if it is 90% jerseys and tees, there is no shorts business here.

candidates.name: Coverage Tier: re-tier the long inseam instead of treating it as the basement
candidates.thesis: Nike's longest, most size-inclusive inseam is also its cheapest, which prices coverage as cheapness for the three groups that most want it - so build a properly constructed 9-11 inch tier in heavyweight mesh with women's grading and extended sizes, and stop letting the retro pole, the modesty need and the plus-size player share the discount rack.
candidates.intersection: inseam price architecture x modest-dress and coverage-first need x plus-size and value replenishment behaviour
candidates.target_consumer: Three groups currently served by the same USD 37 SKU: taller and longer-legged women and modest-dressing athletes who need real coverage; plus-size and big-and-tall players who currently choose AND1 up to 5XL because it is 'affordable and cultural'; and the Gen Z retro buyer for whom 9 inches or longer is the defining spec.
candidates.why_nike: It is a pricing-architecture correction rather than a new product programme, so it is cheap to test: Nike already owns the 11-inch chassis and the Big and Tall grading. It converts a defensive value SKU into a tier with a reason to exist, and it is the one move that serves a Women's Revolution inclusion need and a lifestyle trend with the same block. It also answers a real competitive benchmark - Mitchell and Ness Swingman clears around USD 36 - by competing on construction and grading rather than on nostalgia licence, which Nike does not hold.
candidates.why_hard_to_see: The four facts are each unremarkable alone and only the arrangement is interesting. The 11-inch-at-USD-37 datapoint appears only as skeptic counter-evidence inside two different domains' inseam arguments (A02-S5, A07-S4), where it was used to refute a 'design at the poles' recommendation, not to reveal a pricing inversion. The modesty need sits in a culture signal whose evidence is a decade stale. The plus-size behaviour sits in a consumer signal built on unranked Amazon listings. No domain owns 'price by inseam' as a question, so nobody plotted the line.
candidates.risks: Inseam unit share is unknown in every market, so it is entirely possible the 8-10 inch middle is the volume and the long tier is correctly priced as a value entry. The retro trajectory in 2026 is contested - the same coverage that names baggy live also names micro shorts a top trend, and all the quantitative support for the retro pole was Accio-generated and struck (A05-S3). The coverage-first population has never been sized. And Nike already markets the 11-inch for extra coverage, so this may be a merchandising and grading fix rather than an opportunity worth a line slot.

candidates.name: Legible Function: make the outdoor short readable at three metres on a wholesale rack
candidates.thesis: Nike already ships an outdoor short with UV protection, a phone-secure zip pocket and a durability claim, and seven professional researchers could not find it - so the product problem is not capability but legibility, and the fix is a named outdoor sub-franchise whose abrasion panel, vent zone and pocket ARE the graphic, engineered for a rack with no product copy.
candidates.intersection: an unfindable shipped SKU x the wholesale channel swing x local streetball labels that print function and place on the outside
candidates.target_consumer: The outdoor and streetball player in Greater China, Southeast Asia and the US who is standing at a wholesale rack or scrolling a marketplace listing with no PDP copy, choosing between a Nike short whose function is invisible and a Li-Ning BadFive or Wade UPF short whose function is stated on the garment and in the name.
candidates.why_nike: Nike does not need to invent anything; it needs to stop hiding what it has. That makes this the fastest and cheapest candidate in the portfolio and the one with the clearest internal test - the DNA UV Woven's sell-through in Greater China is a direct read on whether Nike is losing the outdoor player or simply not merchandising to him. It is also the correct response to the channel shift: with Nike Digital down ten consecutive quarters and wholesale growing, the garment must self-merchandise, and Nike's design capability at making function visible is genuinely differentiating against local labels that win on graphics but lack the fabric platform.
candidates.why_hard_to_see: The evidence for it is a negative result distributed across four files, and negatives are invisible to the person producing them. Three domains independently declared an outdoor, storage or UV white space (A03-S7, A06-S4, A07-S8) using the same absent-from-my-snippets reasoning; a fourth domain observed that local labels lead with pockets and place (A07-S9) without connecting it to why Nike's equivalent product was unfindable; a fifth noted the wholesale swing (A02-S7) as a bookings issue. The insight only exists at the level of the whole exercise: the failure of seven researchers is itself the data, and no single researcher could observe their own blind spot.
candidates.risks: This may be a merchandising and marketing programme rather than a product opportunity, which makes it hard to fund as a line slot and easy for a PLM to hand off and lose. It is also possible the incumbent SKU sells poorly on its merits rather than its visibility, and no sell-through data exists either way. In Greater China the route to market is narrowing as Topsports stops selling Nike online by January 2027 (A04-S2), so improved shelf legibility may land on a shrinking shelf. And adidas already merchandises standing Outdoor Basketball and Reflective Shorts collections, so the visible-outdoor position is not unoccupied.

candidates.name: Heat Window: an event-anchored full-price capsule engineered for a late-summer Gulf tournament
candidates.thesis: The only proven antidote in this evidence base to a promotional apparel floor is a major-event story - a competitor grew apparel 35% in one quarter on World Cup demand while its basketball fell 21% - and the SS28 window contains a basketball world championship in the Gulf in late August plus a home Games, so the full-price shorts moment is an event capsule that must also survive 35C-plus heat.
candidates.intersection: a competitor's football-quarter financials x the promotional floor in US wholesale x heat physiology in a market with essentially zero evidence in the base
candidates.target_consumer: Global basketball fans and players buying into a national-team moment - primarily US, European and Asian federation-following consumers - and, on the ground, players and spectators in a Gulf late-August climate where the product has to work at conditions no data in this base has ever measured.
candidates.why_nike: Nike holds federation and national-team relationships and is an outfitter of the US team, so it is one of very few brands that can convert a global event into full-price apparel demand at scale. The mechanism is not speculative: it is documented in this base working for adidas in an adjacent sport in the same fiscal window (A04-S3). It is also the only candidate that gives a shorts buy a reason to sell at full price into the promotional wholesale marketplace the commercial domain identified as its single strongest finding (A04-S4), rather than trying to out-feature a discount.
candidates.why_hard_to_see: Not one of seven specialist files mentions the SS28 calendar, and the audit had to supply it - which means the connection is literally absent from the signal base rather than merely unmade. Worse, the proof of the mechanism was sitting inside the commercial file as a competitor datapoint about FOOTBALL, filed under 'competitors are retreating from basketball', so the one number that shows how to beat a promotional floor was read as evidence about a rival's weakness. A basketball PLM has no reason to read adidas's football apparel quarter, and a commercial analyst had no reason to read it as a calendar instruction.
